1.pericope_label: And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God. For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified

schools.summary: Give the design of the chapter before the verse. It continues the argument of the close of the first chapter, that the gospel does not depend for its success on human wisdom or the philosophy of men; this is confirmed first by the apostle’s own example, having been successful among them and yet not endowed with the graces of elocution, and then, lest the gospel should be thought real folly and be contemned, by showing that it contained true wisdom — a profound scheme, rejected by the men of the world but seen to be wise by those acquainted with its real nature and value. Note the tender and affectionate style of address in And I, brethren. On the second verse, take determined as a fixed, deliberate purpose: it was not a matter of accident or chance that he made Christ his great and constant theme. And it is to be recollected that he formed this resolution knowing the peculiar fondness of the Greeks for subtle disquisitions and for graceful and finished elocution; that he formed it when his own mind, as we may judge from his writings, was strongly inclined by nature to an abstruse and metaphysical kind of discussion, which could not have failed to attract the acute and subtle reasoners of Greece; and that he made it when fully aware that the theme he had chosen would be certain to excite derision and contempt, and yet adhered to it. Take the word know here in the sense of attend to, be engaged in, or regard: I resolved not to give my time and attention while among you to the laws and traditions of the Jews, to your orators, philosophers and poets, to the beauty of your architecture or statuary, to a contemplation of your customs and laws, but to attend to this only — making known the cross of Christ. Elsewhere show how the apostle’s practice matched the principle: he proceeds to show how he personally, in both the matter and the manner of his teaching at Corinth, had acted in accordance with the great principles he has already explained as God’s method; and the testimony of God is his testimony concerning God in Christ. On the second verse, render it better, I did not determine to know: the only subject of teaching concerning which the apostle had formed a determined resolve when coming to Corinth was the preaching of Christ, and of him as being crucified. Here is a statement of what was ever the subject-matter of apostolic teaching. He did not dwell on the miraculous in the life of Christ, which would have pandered to the Jewish longing for a sign; nor did he put forward elaborate theories of the gospel, which would have been a concession to the Greek’s longing after wisdom; but he preached a personal Christ, and especially dwelt on the fact that he had been crucified. We can scarcely realise now the stumbling-block which the preaching of a crucified Christ must have been to Jews and Greeks, the enormous temptation to keep the cross in the background which the early teachers would naturally have felt, and the sublime and confident faith which must have nerved St Paul to make it the central fact of all his teaching. For us the cross is illumined with the glories of eighteen centuries of civilisation, and consecrated with the memory of all that is best and noblest in the history of Christendom; to every Jew and to every Gentile it conveyed but one idea, that of the most revolting and most degrading punishment. The remembrance of this will enable us to realise how uncompromising the apostles’ teaching was, and how it never accommodated itself to any existing desire or prejudice. Elsewhere again keep to the words. Excellency of speech is from an old word meaning preeminence, rising above, found in the inscriptions of Pergamum for persons of position; here it means excess or superfluity — not in excellence of rhetorical display or of philosophical subtlety. On the reading, some manuscripts have the mystery of God, as at verse 7, and others the testimony of God, as at the sixth verse of the first chapter; probably mystery is correct, for Christ crucified is the mystery of God. Paul did not hesitate to appropriate this word, in common use among the mystery religions, but he puts into it his ideas and not those in current use; it is an old word meaning to close, to shut, to initiate, and the papyri give many illustrations of its use for secret doctrines known only to the initiated. This mystery was once hidden from the ages but is now made plain in Christ. On the second verse, note that the negative goes with the verb and not with the pronoun: literally, for I did not decide to know anything among you. Paul means that he did not think it fit, or his business, to know anything for his message beyond this mystery of God. Save Jesus Christ covers both the person and the office; and him crucified is literally, and this one as crucified, a perfect passive participle. This phase in particular was selected by Paul from the start as the centre of his gospel message, and he decided to stick to it even after Athens, where he was practically laughed out of court: the Cross added to the scandal of the Incarnation, but Paul kept to the main track on coming to Corinth.

Say why the apostle turns to his own case. He had begun to speak of his own method of teaching and had straightway fallen into a discussion as to the nature of gospel preaching generally; now again he returns to speak of himself, to show that nothing in him was despised but what belonged to the nature of the gospel itself, and did in a manner adhere to it. He allows therefore that he had not had any of the aids of human eloquence or wisdom to qualify him for producing any effect; but while he acknowledges himself destitute of such resources, he hints at the inference to be drawn from this — that the power of God shone the more illustriously in his ministry, from its standing in no need of such helps. For the present he simply grants that he has nothing of human wisdom. Note that the testimony is to be taken actively, not passively: it is that which has come forth from God, the doctrine of the gospel, of which he is the author and witness; and note the distinction between speech and wisdom, which confirms what was said on the earlier chapter, that he has not been speaking of mere empty prattling, but has included the entire training of human learning. On the second verse, weigh the verb. The Greek word often has the force of choosing out something as precious, and is used elsewhere in the sense of preferring; on that reading the sense is, no kind of knowledge did I hold in esteem — or, supplying a little, nothing did I value myself upon, as worth my knowing, or on the ground of knowledge. Nor is a different interpretation to be altogether rejected, that Paul esteemed nothing as knowledge, or as entitled to be called knowledge, except Christ alone. But whichever is preferred, the substance of the passage amounts to this: as to my wanting the ornaments of speech, and wanting too the more elegant refinements of discourse, the reason was that I did not aspire at them, nay rather, I despised them, because there was one thing only that my heart was set upon — that I might preach Christ with simplicity. Note also what occasions the account: either what was said in the close of the preceding chapter, concerning the choice God has made of the foolish, weak, base and despicable things of the world; or what was declared there, that he was sent to preach the Gospel. And note what the resolution cost: he was well versed in human literature, and had a large compass of knowledge in the things of nature, yet would make known nothing else unto them, nor make anything else the subject of his ministry.

Take the matter first and then the manner. As to the matter or subject, he determined to know nothing among them but Jesus Christ and him crucified — to make a show of no other knowledge than this, to preach nothing, to discover the knowledge of nothing, but Jesus Christ, and him crucified. Note that Christ, in his person and offices, is the sum and substance of the gospel, and ought to be the great subject of a gospel minister’s preaching: his business is to display the banner of the cross, and invite people under it. Anyone that heard Paul preach found him to harp so continually on this string that he would say he knew nothing but Christ and him crucified; whatever other knowledge he had, this was the only knowledge he discovered, and showed himself concerned to propagate among his hearers. As to the manner, take it negatively first. He came not among them with excellency of speech or wisdom; his speech and preaching were not with enticing words of man’s wisdom. He did not affect to appear a fine orator or a deep philosopher, nor did he insinuate himself into their minds by a flourish of words, or a pompous show of deep reason and extraordinary science and skill. He did not set himself to captivate the ear by fine turns and eloquent expressions, nor to please and entertain the fancy with lofty flights of sublime notions. Neither his speech nor the wisdom he taught savoured of human skill: he learnt both in another school.

Give the argument of the chapter, then the apology. The apostle makes an apology for his manner of preaching and gives the reason why he adopted it; he shows that this preaching, notwithstanding it was not with excellence of human speech or wisdom, yet was the mysterious wisdom of God, which the princes of this world did not know, and which the Spirit of God alone could reveal. It is the Spirit of God only that can reveal the things of God; the apostles of Christ know the things of God by the Spirit of God, and teach them, not in the words of man’s wisdom, but in the words of that Spirit; the natural man cannot discern the things of the Spirit, but the spiritual man can discern and teach them, because he has the mind of Christ. On the first verse: when I came to you, acting suitably to my mission, which was to preach the Gospel, but not with human eloquence, I declared to you the testimony, the Gospel, of God — not with excellency of speech, not with arts of rhetoric used by your own philosophers, where the excellence of the speech recommends the matter and compensates for the want of solidity and truth. On the contrary, the testimony concerning Christ and his salvation is so supremely excellent as to dignify any kind of language by which it may be conveyed. I did not affect either deep wisdom or eloquence; and by declaring the testimony of God is meant what God gave me to testify concerning his Son. On the second verse: satisfied that the Gospel of God could alone make you wise unto salvation, I determined to cultivate no other knowledge, and to teach nothing but Jesus Christ, and him crucified, as the foundation of all true wisdom, piety and happiness; no other doctrine shall I proclaim among you. To wave all my other knowledge, and not to preach anything save Jesus Christ and him crucified — that is, what he did, suffered, taught, a part being put for the whole.

Show that the apostle is renewing an attack already won. Nothing was ever more prepared for combat than the spirit of Paul; or rather, I should say, not his spirit, for he was not himself the inventor of these things, but nothing was ever equal to the grace working within him, which overcometh all things. Sufficient indeed is what had been said before to cast down the pride of the boasters about wisdom — nay, even a part of it had been enough; but to enhance the splendour of the victory, he contends anew for the points which he had been affirming, trampling upon the prostrate foe. Look at it in this way. He had brought forward the prophecy which saith, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise. He had shewn the wisdom of God, in that by means of what seemed to be foolishness he destroyed the philosophy of the Gentiles; he had shewn that the foolishness of God is wiser than men; he had shewn that not only did he teach by untaught persons, but also chose untaught persons to learn of him. Now he sheweth that both the thing itself which was preached, and the manner of preaching it, were enough to stagger people, and yet did not stagger them. As thus: not only, saith he, are the disciples uneducated, but I myself also, who am the preacher.

debates: Whether the text reads the testimony of God or the mystery of God.
Whether the negative in verse 2 governs the verb or the object.
What excellency of speech excludes.
What it cost to preach a crucified Christ at Corinth.
outliers: Robertson prefers the reading mystery of God and connects the word to the mystery religions.
Ellicott renders the verse, I did not determine to know, moving the negative off the object.
Calvin weighs the Greek verb as meaning to esteem or prefer rather than to resolve.
Chrysostom reads the chapter as a second assault on an enemy already prostrate.

3.pericope_label: And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling. And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power: that your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God

schools.summary: Set the weakness in its circumstances. He continued at Corinth a year and six months, in conscious feebleness, diffident of his own powers and not trusting to his own strength; he was sensible that he had many enemies to encounter, and sensible of his own natural disadvantages as a public speaker; he knew how much the Greeks valued a manly and elegant species of oratory, and therefore delivered his message with deep and anxious solicitude as to the result. It was at this time, and in view of these circumstances, that the Lord spoke to him by night in a vision and said, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace, for I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee, for I have much people in this city. Draw the pastoral inference: if Paul was conscious of weakness, well may other ministers be; and if Paul sometimes trembled in deep solicitude about the result of his message, well may other ministers tremble also. It is when ministers go to their work conscious of their own weakness, burdened with the weight of their message and deeply solicitous about the result, that the promises of the gospel are inestimably precious, and then, perhaps then only, that they are successful. On the fourth verse, distinguish speech from preaching: the former refers perhaps to his more private reasonings, the latter to his public discourses. Not with enticing words means not with persuasive reasonings, not with that kind of oratory adapted to captivate and charm, which the Greeks so much esteemed. Demonstration means the showing, the testimony or evidence which the Spirit produced: the Spirit furnished the evidence of the divine origin of the religion he preached, and it did not depend for its proof on his own reasonings or eloquence. That demonstration was the miracles wrought, the gift of tongues, and the remarkable conversions which attended the gospel; and the power is the power of God, whose effects are the evidence to which the apostle appeals — the conversion of sinners of all classes, ages and conditions when all human means of reforming them was vain, and the giving them peace and joy, and the transforming of their lives. On the fifth verse, faith means the belief of the divine origin of the Christian religion; should not stand is in Greek should not be, that is, should not rest or be sustained upon this. God intended to furnish a firm and solid demonstration that the religion they embraced was from him, and this could not be if the preaching had been attended with the graces of eloquence or the abstractions of refined metaphysical reasoning, for it would then appear to rest on human wisdom. Every Christian has thus, in his own experience, furnished demonstration that the religion which he loves is from God: man could not subdue those sins, and man could not so entirely transform the soul. Elsewhere read the weakness psychologically. To show that the real force of his teaching lay in its subject-matter, and not in any power with which he proclaimed the gospel, the apostle dwells upon his own physical weakness; and the weakness and fear and trembling had in it probably a large element of that self-distrust which so noble and sensitive a nature would feel in the fulfilment of so exalted a mission. But the allusion is not only to that: there is a reference also to what we may call a physical apprehension of danger. The bravest are not those who do not experience any sensation of fear, but rather those who keenly appreciate danger, who have an instinctive shrinking from it, and yet eventually by their moral might conquer this dread; and there are traces of this element in his character elsewhere — Be not afraid, when he was labouring at Corinth; Be of good cheer, Paul, when the terrible scene before Ananias had depressed him; Fear not, Paul, when the angel appeared to him amid the storm and shipwreck. The result which necessarily followed from this weakness and trembling was that neither his speech, that is the style of his teaching, nor his preaching, that is its subject-matter, was of such a kind as to appeal to the natural tastes of the Corinthians. His demonstration of the truth of the gospel was the result of no human art or skill, but came from the Spirit and power of God; and therefore the Corinthians could glory in no human teacher, but only in the power of God, which was the true source of the success of the gospel amongst them. Elsewhere again keep to the words. I was with you is rather, I came to you: I not only eschewed all affectation of cleverness or grandiloquence, but went to the opposite extreme of diffidence and nervous self-effacement. Paul had been in prison in Philippi, driven out of Thessalonica and Beroea, politely bowed out of Athens; it is a human touch to see this shrinking as he faced the hard conditions in Corinth, and it is a common feeling of the most effective preachers, for cool complacency is not the mood of the finest preaching. On enticing words, admit that the disclaimer looks false, or like mock modesty, since surely the preacher desires to be persuasive; but the adjective has not yet been found elsewhere and seems formed directly from the verb to persuade. The kindred noun is used of the specious and plausible Gnostic philosophers, and gullible people are easy marks for these plausible pulpiteers — Corinth put a premium on the veneer of false rhetoric and thin thinking. Demonstration is an old word occurring nowhere else in the New Testament, standing in contrast with the plausibility just mentioned; Spirit here may be the Holy Spirit or the inward spirit as opposed to superficial expression, and power is moral power rather than intellectual acuteness. On the fifth verse, note that the only secure place for faith to find a rest is in God’s power, not in the wisdom of men: one has only to instance the changing theories of men about science, philosophy, religion and politics to see this, for a sure word from God can be depended on.

Name the weakness and then turn it into the argument. It may mean the weakness of his bodily presence, the contemptibleness of his voice, and the mean figure he made as a preacher among them, both in the matter and the manner of his ministry; or his lowly and humble deportment, not exerting the power and authority Christ had given him as an apostle, but choosing rather to work with his own hands, as he did at Corinth, to minister to his own necessities and those of others; or the many persecutions he endured there for the sake of preaching a crucified Christ, which he sometimes calls infirmities. Then explain at greater length what he had previously touched upon — that he had nothing shining or excellent in him in the eyes of men to raise him to distinction. He concedes to his adversaries what they desired, but in such a way as to make those very things which in their opinion tended to detract from the credit of his ministry redound to its highest commendation: if he appeared less worthy of esteem from being so mean and abject according to the flesh, the power of God shone out the more conspicuously in this, that he could effect so much while sustained by no human helps. He has in his eye not merely the foolish boasters who aimed at mere show, with a view to obtaining a name, but the Corinthians too, who gazed with astonishment on their empty shows; and a recital of this kind was fitted to have great weight with them, since they were aware that Paul had brought nothing with him in respect of the flesh that was fitted to help him forward, and yet they had seen the amazing success which the Lord vouchsafed to his preaching, and had in a manner beheld with their own eyes the Spirit of God present in his doctrine. On the fourth verse, by enticing words understand that exquisite oratory which aims and strives rather by artifice than by truth, and an appearance of refinement that allures the minds of men. It is not without good reason that persuasiveness is ascribed to human wisdom: for the word of the Lord constrains us by its majesty, as if by a violent impulse, to yield obedience to it, whereas human wisdom has her allurements, by which she insinuates herself, and her blandishments, by which she may conciliate the affections of her hearers. Note that the adjective occurs nowhere else in the New Testament or in classical authors, so that some suppose a corruption of the reading. With this he contrasts the demonstration, which most interpreters consider as restricted to miracles; but take it in a more general sense, as meaning the hand of God powerfully exercised. On the fifth verse, say what the Corinthians derived from it: that their faith was founded not on men but on God. If the apostle’s preaching had rested exclusively on the power of eloquence, it might have been overthrown by superior eloquence, and besides, no one would pronounce that to be solid truth which rests on mere elegance of speech. On the other hand, that must have been most powerful which could stand of itself without any foreign aid; and it forms a choice commendation of Paul’s preaching that heavenly influence shone forth in it so clearly that it surmounted so many hindrances while deriving no assistance from the world. It follows that they must not allow themselves to be moved away from his doctrine, which they acknowledge to rest on the authority of God. Let it be known by us that it is the property of faith to rest upon God alone, without depending on men; for it requires so much certainty to go upon that it will not fail even when assailed by all the machinations of hell, but will perseveringly endure and sustain every assault. This cannot be accomplished unless we are fully persuaded that God has spoken to us, and that what we have believed is no mere contrivance of men. Note also, on the fifth verse, that the Spirit directed him to this way of preaching with this view: that faith in Christ, which comes by hearing, might not be attributed to the force of human eloquence and oratory, nor stand upon so sandy a foundation as might be puffed away by a superior flow and force of words, but be ascribed, as it ought, to almighty power.

Guess at the infirmity, and then show what follows from it. It is very likely that St Paul had not only something in his speech very unfavourable to a ready and powerful elocution, but also some infirmity of body that was still more disadvantageous. A fine appearance and a fine voice cover many weaknesses and defects, and strongly recommend what is spoken, though it be not remarkable for depth of thought or solidity of reasoning; many popular orators have little besides their persons and their voice to recommend them. Louis the Fourteenth styled Peter du Bosc the finest speaker in his kingdom, and among his own people he was styled the perfect orator; look at the works of this French protestant divine and you find it difficult to subscribe to the above sayings, and the difficulty is solved by the information that his person was noble and princely and his voice full, harmonious and majestic. Paul had none of these advantages, and yet idolatry and superstition fell before him: thus God was seen in the work, and the man was forgotten. On the fear and much trembling, say this was often the state of his mind, dreading lest he should at any time be unfaithful and so grieve the Spirit of God, or that, after having preached to others, himself should be a castaway; and add the maxim, that an eminent divine has said it requires three things to make a good preacher — study, temptation and prayer. Take the fear also as lest he should offend any, and the much trembling as the emotion of his mind affecting his very body. On the fourth verse, distinguish the terms: his speech is his doctrine, the matter of his preaching, and his preaching is his proclamation, his manner of recommending the grand but simple truths of the Gospel. Not with enticing words means with persuasive doctrines of human wisdom: in every case I left man out, that God might become the more evident, and I used none of the means by which great orators become popular and gain fame. Demonstration means the manifestation — or, as two ancient manuscripts have it, the revelation — of the Spirit: the doctrine he preached was revealed by the Spirit, and that it was so was made manifest by the holiness, purity and usefulness of the doctrine, while the overthrow of idolatry and the conversion of souls by the power and energy of the preaching were the demonstration that all was divine. Note that the greater part of the best manuscripts, versions and fathers leave out the adjective man’s before wisdom, though it is necessarily implied. Say that the demonstration is the powerful kind which flows from the Holy Spirit, working on the conscience with the most convincing light and the most persuasive evidence. On the fifth verse: that the illumination of your souls and your conversion to God might appear to have nothing human in it, your belief is founded not in human wisdom but in divine power. Human wisdom was not employed, and human power, if it had been employed, could not have produced the change.

Use the verse as a proof, not as a text to expound. That Paul was full of the Holy Ghost, and all his fellow Apostles, and they who after them believed in Father, Son and Holy Ghost, hear from himself as he writes plainly in his Epistles: And my speech, he says, and my preaching was not in persuasive words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power. And again, He who sealed us for this very purpose is God, who gave us the earnest of the Spirit. And again, He that raised up Jesus from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit which dwelleth in you. And again, writing to Timothy, That good thing which was committed to thee guard through the Holy Ghost which was given to us.

debates: What the weakness, fear and trembling were.
Whether the demonstration of the Spirit means miracles only.
What the rare adjective rendered enticing means, and whether the text is sound.
What it means for faith to stand in the power of God rather than the wisdom of men.
outliers: Ellicott reads a physical apprehension of danger into the fear, and traces it through three encouragements in Acts.
Clarke illustrates the apostle’s disadvantages by the person and voice of a French court preacher.
Calvin refuses to restrict the demonstration of the Spirit to miracles.
Cyril cites the verse as evidence that Paul was full of the Holy Ghost, without expounding it.

6.pericope_label: Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought

schools.summary: Mark the turn in the argument. This commences the second head of the chapter, in which the apostle shows that if human wisdom is wanting in his preaching, it is not devoid of true and solid and even divine wisdom. We speak wisdom means, we do not admit that we utter foolishness: we have spoken of the foolishness of preaching, and of the estimate in which it was held by the world, and of our own manner among you as not laying claim to human learning or eloquence; but we do not mean to admit that we have really been speaking folly. On the perfect, the word is applied to Christians, as elsewhere when the apostle says, let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded; and it denotes those who were advanced in Christian knowledge, qualified to understand the subject, who had made progress in the knowledge of the mysteries of the gospel and so saw its excellence. It does not mean here that they were sinless, for the argument does not bear on that inquiry, but that they were qualified to understand the gospel, in contradistinction from the gross, the sensual and the carnally minded, who rejected it as foolishness. There is perhaps an allusion to the heathen mysteries, where those who had been fully initiated were said to be perfect, fully instructed in those rites and doctrines. Elsewhere sharpen the contrast: there is a wisdom in the gospel, and the assertion is in the Greek a more striking contrast to the fourth verse than appears in the English, for there the word is simply wisdom and not man’s wisdom, so that this statement is a verbal contradiction of that one. In using the plural we, the apostle implies that he did not stand alone among the Apostles in his method of teaching. The perfect are those who are grown up, and not babes; the wisdom of the gospel is that deep spiritual truth which only those whose spiritual natures have been trained and cultivated were capable of understanding. This wisdom, however, the Apostle had not taught the Corinthians: he had only taught them the alphabet of Christianity, for they were still but babes, still only fleshly. That he himself not only grasped the higher truths which he designates the wisdom of the gospel, but taught them gladly where there were hearers capable of appreciating them, is evident from many passages in the Epistles to the Romans, Colossians and Ephesians, where he unfolds the mysteries of the gospel. Read the last clause, better, which are being brought to nought, the reference being not to the inherent transitoriness of human wisdom and teachers, but to the fact that they are being brought to nought by God’s rejection of them and his choice of the weak things as the means of spreading the gospel. Elsewhere again, guard against the wrong parallel. Paul is not here drawing a distinction between exoteric and esoteric wisdom, as the Gnostics did for their initiates, but simply marking the necessary difference in teaching for babes and for adults or grown men, this being the common use of the word for relative perfection. Some were simply old babes, unable in spite of their years to digest solid spiritual food — the ample teaching as to the Person of Christ and the eternal purpose of God, such wisdom as we have in the Epistles to the Ephesians and the Colossians especially, and in a less degree in the Epistle to the Romans, and as is discerned in the Gospel of John compared with the other Evangelists. These imperfect disciples Paul wishes to develop into spiritual maturity. Of this world is more exactly of this age: this wisdom does not belong to the passing age of fleeting things, but to the enduring and eternal. And the participle rendered which are coming to naught is present passive: the gradual nullification of these rulers before the final and certain triumph of the power of Christ in his kingdom.

Guard against two misreadings at once. Lest he should appear to despise wisdom, or to condemn learning with a sort of barbarian ferocity, he adds that he is not devoid of wisdom which was worthy of the name, but was esteemed as such by none but competent judges. By those that were perfect he means not those who had attained a wisdom that was full and complete, but those who possess a sound and unbiased judgment: the Hebrew word which the Septuagint renders by this Greek one is used of Jacob as a plain man, without any manifest blemish, and its cognate is frequently applied to the sacrificial victims to denote that they were without spot. He twits in passing those who had no relish for his preaching, and gives them to understand that it was owing to their own fault: if my doctrine is disrelished by any of you, those persons give sufficient evidence from that very token that they possess a depraved and vitiated understanding, inasmuch as it will invariably be acknowledged to be the highest wisdom among men of sound intellect and correct judgment. While Paul’s preaching was open to the view of all, it was nevertheless not always estimated according to its value, and this is the reason why he appeals to sound and unbiased judges — he does not submit the case to every one, but appeals to competent judges — who would declare that doctrine, which the world accounted insipid, to be true wisdom. Meanwhile, by the words we speak wisdom, he intimates that he set before them an elegant specimen of admirable wisdom, lest any one should allege that he boasted of a thing unknown. Note also the occasion of the vindication: though the wise philosophers among the Gentiles accounted the Gospel foolishness, and though the apostle, by an ironical concession, had called the ministry of it the foolishness of preaching and the foolishness of God, and had thought best for wise reasons to deliver it in a plain and simple manner, without the embellishments of human wisdom, yet he vindicates it from the charge of folly. It was not folly, but wisdom, which he and his fellow ministers preached, and that of the highest kind, though it was not esteemed so by all men.

Show what he did bring them, having said what he did not. Though he had not come to them with the excellency of human wisdom, with any of the boasted knowledge and literature of the Jews or Greeks, yet he had communicated to them a treasure of the truest and the highest wisdom: we speak wisdom among those who are perfect, among those who are well instructed in Christianity and come to some maturity in the things of God. Those that receive the doctrine as divine, and, having been illuminated by the Holy Spirit, have looked well into it, discover true wisdom in it: they not only understand the plain history of Christ, and him crucified, but discern the deep and admirable designs of the divine wisdom therein. Though what we preach is foolishness to the world, it is wisdom to them; they are made wise by it, and can discern wisdom in it. Note that those who are wise themselves are the only proper judges of what is wisdom — not indeed the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, but the wisdom of God in a mystery; not worldly wisdom, but divine; not such as the men of this world could have discovered, nor such as worldly men, under the direction of pride and passion and appetite and worldly interest, and destitute of the Spirit of God, can receive. Note how different is the judgment of God from that of the world: he seeth not as man seeth. The wisdom he teaches is of a quite different kind from what passes under that notion in the world — not the wisdom of politicians, nor philosophers, nor rabbis, not such as they teach nor such as they relish, but the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom of God.

Define the perfect, then sort the wisdoms. By those that are perfect we are to understand Christians of the highest knowledge and attainments, those who were fully instructed in the knowledge of God through Christ Jesus; nothing else deserved the name of wisdom. And though he apologises for not coming to them with excellency of speech or wisdom, he means what was reputed wisdom among the Greeks, which in the sight of God was mere folly compared with the wisdom that came from above. Then distinguish a fourfold wisdom. First, heathen wisdom, that of the Gentile philosophers, which the Jews termed Grecian wisdom, and which they so undervalued that they joined two things under the same curse: cursed is he that breeds hogs, and cursed is he who teaches his son Grecian wisdom. Second, Jewish wisdom, that of the scribes and Pharisees, who crucified our Lord. Third, the Gospel, which is called the wisdom of God in a mystery. Fourth, the wisdom of this world, that system of knowledge which the Jews made up out of the writings of their scribes and doctors; and note that this state is called by them this or the present world, to distinguish it from the world to come, that is, the days of the Messiah. Whether we understand the term this world as relating to the state of the Gentiles, cultivated to the uttermost in philosophical learning, or to the then state of the Jews, who had made the word of God of no effect by their traditions, the wisdom meant is one that comes to nought. Elsewhere put it shortly: yea, the truest and most excellent wisdom, spoken among the perfect, that is, adult and experienced Christians; and by wisdom here he seems to mean not the whole Christian doctrine, but the most sublime and abstruse parts of it — not the wisdom admired and taught by the men of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, Jewish or heathen, that come to nought, both they and their wisdom, and the world itself.

Answer the charge of foolishness with a comparison. Darkness seems to be more suitable than light to those that are diseased in their eyesight, wherefore they betake themselves by preference to some room that is thoroughly shaded over; and this also is the case with the wisdom which is spiritual. As the wisdom which is of God seemed to be foolishness unto those without, so their own wisdom, being foolishness indeed, was accounted by them wisdom. The result has been just as if a man having skill in navigation were to promise that without a ship or sails he would pass over a boundless tract of sea, and then endeavour by reasonings to prove that the thing is possible; but some other person, ignorant of it all, committing himself to a ship and a steersman and sailors, were thus to sail in safety. For the seeming ignorance of this man is wiser than the wisdom of the other. Excellent is the art of managing a ship, but when it makes too great professions it is a kind of folly; and so is every art which is not contented with its own proper limits. Just so the wisdom which is without would be wisdom indeed if it had had the benefit of the Spirit; but since it trusted all to itself and supposed that it wanted none of that help, it became foolishness, although it seemed to be wisdom. Note the order of the argument: having first exposed it by the facts, then and not till then he calls it foolishness; and having first called the wisdom of God folly, according to their reckoning, then and not till then he shews it to be wisdom — for after our proofs, not before, we are best able to abash the gainsayers.

debates: Who the perfect are: the mature, the initiated, or those of sound judgment.
Whether the wisdom spoken among the perfect had been taught at Corinth at all.
Whether the wisdom of this world means Greek philosophy, rabbinic tradition, or both.
Whether the rulers are coming to nought by nature or by God’s rejection.
outliers: Calvin makes the perfect those of sound and unbiased judgment rather than the advanced.
Ellicott holds that the wisdom of this verse was never taught to the Corinthians at all.
Robertson denies any parallel with the Gnostic distinction between exoteric and esoteric teaching.
Chrysostom answers the charge with a parable of a navigator who promises to cross the sea without a ship.

7.pericope_label: But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory: which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory

schools.summary: Correct the translation first. The words even and wisdom were supplied by the translators, and the sense would be more perspicuous if they were omitted and the rendering made literally: we proclaim the divine wisdom hidden in a mystery. The apostle does not say that their preaching was mysterious, nor that their doctrine was unintelligible; he refers to the fact that this wisdom had been hidden in a mystery from men until that time, but was then revealed by the gospel. The word mystery with us is commonly used in the sense of that which is beyond comprehension, and is often applied to doctrines which exhibit difficulties we are not able to explain; but this is not the sense in which it is commonly used in the Scriptures, where the word properly denotes that which is concealed or hidden. On the princes, understand those engaged in the crucifixion of the Messiah, referring both to the Jewish rulers and to the Roman governor. They did not perceive or appreciate the excellency of his character, the wisdom of his plan, the glory of his scheme of salvation; their ignorance arose from not understanding the prophecies, and from an unwillingness to be convinced that Jesus of Nazareth had been truly sent by God, as Peter says that it was through ignorance that the Jews had put him to death. Had they fully understood his character, and seen the wisdom of his plan, they would not have put him to death: it is incredible that they would have crucified their Messiah, knowing him to be such. They might have known it, but they were unwilling to examine the evidence; they expected a different Messiah, and were unwilling to admit the claims of Jesus of Nazareth. For this ignorance, however, there was no excuse: if they had not a full knowledge, it was their own fault, since the miracles were a complete attestation of his divine mission. Elsewhere explain the method rather than the word. In a mystery describes the plan on which his speaking of God’s wisdom proceeded: he dealt with it as the ancient mysteries were dealt with, explaining certain truths only to the initiated, and not to all. Hidden means heretofore unrevealed, but now made manifest in Christ and by his teachers; and this has been in accordance with what God ordained before the beginning of time, to our glory, as distinct from the humiliation of the world’s teaching, which is coming to nought. On the eighth verse, say that the conduct of the princes and rulers of this world, alike Jewish and Gentile, illustrates and proves the previous assertion; and that the Lord of glory stands in striking contrast to the ignominy of the crucifixion. Elsewhere again keep to the grammar. Two points are sharply made: it is God’s wisdom, note the emphatic position of the genitive, in contrast to the wisdom of this age — every age of the world has a conceit of its own, and it is particularly true of this twentieth century, but God’s wisdom is eternal and superior to the wisdom of any age or time, and alone absolute. It is not certain whether in a mystery is to be taken with wisdom or with we speak; the result does not differ greatly, and probably it goes with wisdom, so long a secret and now at last revealed. That hath been hidden is an articular perfect passive participle, more precisely defining the indefinite noun. Foreordained before the worlds is a constative aorist of God’s elective purpose as shown in Christ crucified — it was no afterthought or change of plan. Unto our glory is the glory of inward enlightenment as well as of outward exaltation. On the eighth verse: knoweth is a perfect active, has known, has discerned — they have shown amazing ignorance of God’s wisdom; had they known it is a condition of the second class, determined as unfulfilled. Peter in the great sermon at Pentecost commented on the ignorance of the Jews in crucifying Christ as the only hope for repentance on their part. The Lord of glory is a genitive meaning characterised by glory, bringing out the contrast between the indignity of the Cross and the majesty of the Victim.

Say whose wisdom it is, and then why it is despised. It is not of men, not of the wise politicians, the learned philosophers and Rabbins; human wisdom has no hand in forming it, nor in revealing it, nor in propagating it, and it is disliked and disapproved by it. The Gospel is the sole produce of divine wisdom, and in it there is a glorious display of that wisdom, even in those doctrines which are most charged with folly — salvation by a crucified Christ, justification by his righteousness, pardon by his blood, satisfaction by his sacrifice. Then assign the reason why the doctrine of the gospel is not held in high esteem by the world: because it is involved in mysteries. For the gospel so far transcends the perspicacity of human intellect that, to whatever height those who are accounted men of superior intellect may raise their view, they never can reach its elevated height, while in the meantime they despise its meanness, as if it were prostrate at their feet; and the consequence is that the more proudly they contemn it, the farther they are from acquaintance with it — nay more, they are removed to so great a distance as to be prevented from even seeing it. Then meet the danger this raises. Paul having said that the gospel was a hidden thing, there was a danger lest believers should, on hearing this, be appalled by the difficulty and retire in despair; accordingly he declares that it had notwithstanding been appointed to us, that we might enjoy it. Lest any one should reckon that he has nothing to do with it, or imagine it unlawful to direct his eyes towards it as not being within the reach of human capacity, he teaches that it has been communicated to us in accordance with the eternal counsel of God; and by an implied comparison he extols that grace which has been opened up by Christ’s advent, and distinguishes us above our fathers, who lived under the law. On the eighth verse, take the negative broadly. Scripture is wont to speak in terms of universality of those things that happen for the most part, and to make a negative statement in the same terms as to those things that happen only in a few cases; in this sense there is nothing inconsistent with the statement, though there were found a few men of distinction, elevated above others in point of dignity, who were at the same time endowed with the pure knowledge of God. The wisdom of God shone forth clearly, and yet the princes did not perceive it: those who took the lead in the crucifixion of Christ were on the one hand the chief men of the Jews, high in credit for holiness and wisdom, and on the other hand Pilate and the Roman empire; and in this we have a most distinct proof of the utter blindness of all that are wise only according to the flesh. Note also who the princes are not: not the devils, as some have thought, who had they known what God designed to do by the death of Christ would never have been concerned in bringing it about; nor so much the political governors of the Roman empire, as Herod and Pontius Pilate, who were also entirely ignorant of it; but rather the ecclesiastical rulers of the Jewish church state, the priests, Scribes and Pharisees, the Rabbins and learned doctors, who knew nothing of the wisdom of the Gospel, nor the Messiah when he came, nor the prophecies concerning him.

Date the concealment and name the concealers. The wisdom of God in a mystery is the Gospel of Jesus Christ, which had been comparatively hidden from the foundation of the world — that is, the settling of the Jewish economy, as this phrase often means — though appointed from the beginning to be revealed in the fullness of time. For though this Gospel was in a certain sense announced by the prophets and prefigured by the law, it is certain that even the most intelligent of the Jewish rulers, their doctors, scribes and Pharisees, had no adequate knowledge of it; therefore it was still a mystery to them and to others, till it was so gloriously revealed by the preaching of the apostles. On the eighth verse it is evident that this world refers to the Jewish state, and to the degree of knowledge in that state, and the rulers are the priests, rabbins and the rest, who were principally concerned in the crucifixion of our Lord. The Lord of glory means the glorious Lord, infinitely transcending all the rulers of the universe, whose is eternal glory, who gave that glorious Gospel in which his followers may glory, as it affords them such cause of triumph as the heathens had not, who gloried in their philosophers: here is a teacher come from God, who has taught the most glorious truths it is possible for the soul of man to conceive, and has promised to lead all the followers of his crucified Master to that state of glory which is ineffable and eternal. Elsewhere put it shortly: we speak the mysterious wisdom of God, which was hidden for many ages from all the world, and is still hidden even from babes in Christ, much more from all unbelievers. Which God ordained before the world — so far is this from coming to nought, like worldly wisdom; and for our glory, arising from the glory of our Lord, and then to be revealed when all worldly glory vanishes. On the eighth verse, they would not have crucified, that is, punished as a slave, the Lord of glory. The giving of Christ this august title, peculiar to the great Jehovah, plainly shows him to be the supreme God; in like manner the Father is styled the Father of glory, and the Holy Ghost the Spirit of glory, and the application of this title to all the three shows that Father, Son and Holy Ghost are the God of glory, as the only true God is elsewhere called.

debates: Whether a mystery means something incomprehensible or something formerly concealed.
Whether in a mystery attaches to the wisdom or to the speaking.
Who the princes of this world are: demons, Roman governors, or Jewish rulers.
Whether their ignorance excuses them.
outliers: Ellicott makes the mystery a method of teaching, on the model of the ancient mysteries.
Barnes denies that mystery in Scripture means what is beyond comprehension.
Calvin reads the denial as a general statement, leaving room for a few rulers who did know God.
Wesley takes the Lord of glory as a proof of the divinity of Christ and of the Trinity.

9.pericope_label: But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit: for the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God

schools.summary: Trace the quotation, then refuse the popular application. The passage is from Isaiah, not quoted literally, but the sense only given; the words are found in the apocryphal books of Elijah, and some early writers supposed Paul quoted from those, but it is evident he had the passage in Isaiah in his eye. These words are often applied to the future life, and supposed to describe the state of the blessed there; but against the supposition that they refer directly to the future state there are insuperable objections. First, the passage in Isaiah has no such reference: there it is designed to describe the blessedness of those admitted to the divine favour, who had communion with God and to whom God manifested himself as their Friend, a blessedness said to be superior to all that men elsewhere enjoy. Secondly, the object of the apostle here is not to describe the future state of the redeemed, but to prove that those who are Christians have true wisdom. On the tenth verse, note that it commences the third part of the chapter, showing how these truths, so full of wisdom, had been communicated to Christians: not by any native endowments of theirs, nor by any strength of faculties or powers, but solely by revelation from God. Unto us means first to the apostles; secondly, to the church and the world through their inspired instructors; and thirdly, to all Christians by the illuminating agency of the Spirit on their hearts. The connexion shows he did not mean to confine the declaration to the apostles merely, for his design was to show that all Christians have this true wisdom: no truth is communicated to Christians now which was not revealed to and by the inspired writers, but the same truths are imparted by means of their writings and by the illumination of the Spirit to all the true friends of God. Elsewhere face the difficulty of the citation squarely. Where do the words occur? They are not to be found as here given anywhere in the Old Testament. It has therefore been suggested that they are from some apocryphal book, or some book which has been lost; another suggestion is that the reference is not to a writing at all, but to historical facts. None of these explanations would justify the use of the phrase, it is written, which in the apostolic writings is confined to quotations from the Old Testament scriptures, and is not used where the words are taken from other sources. Although the words given here are not to be found in the same sequence in any passage of the Old Testament, still there are phrases scattered through the writings of Isaiah which would easily be joined together in memory and resemble even verbally the passage as written here by the Apostle. This is not the only place in which St Paul would seem thus to refer to the Old Testament when he is not basing any argument upon a particular sentence, but merely availing himself of some thoughts or words as an illustration of a truth he is enforcing. On the tenth verse, the emphatic word is us: none of the princes of this age know these things, but God hath revealed them unto us his apostles and teachers, and this revelation of spiritual truth is made by the Holy Spirit of God to our spirits. The Apostle gives two proofs that the Apostles have this knowledge and that the Holy Spirit is its source: first, because the Holy Spirit alone is capable of imparting this knowledge, and second, because the Holy Spirit has been given to us. Searcheth does not convey the idea of inquiry for the purpose of acquiring knowledge, but rather complete and accurate knowledge itself. Elsewhere again keep to the words. It is not certain where Paul derives this quotation as Scripture; it is likely that he combines freely three passages of Isaiah in a sort of catena or free chain of quotations, as he does elsewhere. There is an anacoluthon, since the relative occurs as direct object with saw and heard, but as subject with entered. Prepared is the only instance where Paul uses this verb of God, though it occurs of final glory and of final misery; but here undoubtedly the dominant idea is the present blessing to those who love God. On the tenth verse, note the reading: for God revealed unto us, rather than but — the one is superficially easier, the other intrinsically better. Paul explains why this is no longer hidden, and we do not have to wait for heaven to see these things. The revelation took place at the entry of the Gospel into the world, not when we were admitted into the Church or baptized; the Holy Spirit is the agent of it, a revelation with a definite beginning, an unveiling by the Spirit where human ability and research would not have sufficed. The verb searcheth occurs in the papyri for a professional searcher’s report and for searchers employed as customs officials: the Spirit is the organ of understanding between man and God.

State the two difficulties before expounding. All are agreed that the passage is taken from Isaiah, and as the meaning is at first view plain and easy, interpreters do not give themselves much trouble in expounding it; but on looking more narrowly into it, two very great difficulties present themselves. The first is that the words here quoted by Paul do not correspond with the words of the Prophet. The second is that it seems as though Paul had perverted the Prophet’s declaration to a purpose quite foreign to his design. As to the words, they may be taken in different senses and are explained variously by interpreters: some render the passage as saying that from the beginning of the world men have not heard, nor perceived with their ears, and eye hath not seen any god beside thee who doth act in such a manner towards him that waiteth for him; others understand the discourse as addressed to God, that eye hath not seen, nor hath ear heard, O God, besides thee, the things which thou dost for those that wait for thee. Then say what the words are applied to here: not the glories and happiness of the future state, though these are indeed invisible, unheard of, and inconceivable as to the excellency and fulness of them, and are what God has prepared from all eternity for all those on whom he bestows his grace here; but the doctrines of grace and the mysteries of the Gospel, as the context and the reason of their citation abundantly show. On the tenth verse, meet the objection: since this wisdom is so hidden and mysterious, and the doctrines of the Gospel so much out of the sight and understanding of men, how come any to be acquainted with them? The answer is ready: God has made a revelation of them, not only in his word, which is common to men, nor only to his ministers, but to private Christians and believers. Then give the doctrine. Having shut up all mankind in blindness, and having taken away from the human intellect the power of attaining to a knowledge of God by its own resources, he now shows in what way believers are exempted from this blindness — by the Lord’s honouring them with a special illumination of the Spirit. Hence the greater the bluntness of the human intellect for understanding the mysteries of God, and the greater the uncertainty under which it labours, so much the surer is our faith, which rests for its support on the revelation of God’s Spirit; and in this too we recognise the unbounded goodness of God, who makes our defect contribute to our advantage. This is added for the consolation of the pious, that they may rest more securely in the revelation which they have from the Spirit of God, as though he had said, let it suffice us to have the Spirit of God as a witness, for there is nothing in God that is too profound for him to reach. By the deep things you must understand not secret judgments, which we are forbidden to search, but the entire doctrine of salvation, which would have been to no purpose set before us in the Scriptures were it not that God elevates our minds to it by his Spirit.

Take the verse as testimony to the Spirit. God has revealed true wisdom to us by his Spirit, and here is a proof of the divine authority of the Holy Scriptures. In proof of the Divinity of the Holy Ghost, observe that he knows all things, and searches all things, even the deep things of God: no one can know the things of God but his Holy Spirit, who is one with the Father and the Son, and who makes known divine mysteries to his church. This is most clear testimony, both to the real Godhead and to the distinct person of the Holy Spirit. The apostles were not guided by worldly principles: they had the revelation of these things from the Spirit of God, and the saving impression of them from the same Spirit; and these things they declared in plain, simple language taught by the Holy Spirit, totally different from the affected oratory or enticing words of man’s wisdom.

Fix the reference of the quotation and then the revelation. The quotation is taken from Isaiah, and the sense is continued from the seventh verse, we speak being understood: we do not preach the wisdom of this world, but that mysterious wisdom of God of which the prophet said, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. These words have been applied to the state of glory in a future world, but they certainly belong to the present state, and express merely the wondrous light, life and liberty which the Gospel communicates to them that believe in the Lord Jesus Christ in the way the Gospel itself requires. To this the prophet himself refers, and it is evident from the following verse that the apostle also refers to the same thing. Such a scheme of salvation, in which God’s glory and man’s felicity should be equally secured, had never been seen, never heard of, nor could any mind but that of God have conceived the idea of so vast a project, nor any power but his own have brought it to effect. On the tenth verse, take the revelation as a manifest proof that the apostle speaks here of the glories of the Gospel, and not of the glories of the future world. The Spirit that searcheth all things is the Spirit of God, which spoke by the prophets and has now given to the apostles the fullness of that heavenly truth, of which he gave to the former only the outlines. It is only the Spirit of God that can reveal the counsels of God: these are the purposes which have existed in his infinite wisdom and goodness from eternity, and particularly what refers to creation, providence, redemption and eternal glory, as far as men and angels are concerned in them. The apostles were so fully convinced that the scheme of redemption proclaimed by the Gospel was divine that they boldly asserted that these things infinitely surpassed the wisdom and comprehension of man. God was now in a certain way become manifest: many attributes of his, which to the heathen world would have for ever lain in obscurity, were now not only brought to light as existing in him, but illustrated by the gracious displays which he had made of himself. Add that the ignorance of the princes fulfils what is written concerning the blessings of the Messiah’s kingdom, and that no natural man hath either seen, heard or known the things God hath prepared; and that the Spirit searcheth even the deep things of God, be they ever so hidden and mysterious — the depths both of his nature and of his kingdom.

Use the verse first to bound what may be known. One God there is, everywhere present, beholding all things, perceiving all things, creating all things through Christ; a fountain of every good, abundant and unfailing, a river of blessings, an eternal light of never-failing splendour, an insuperable power condescending to our infirmities, whose very Name we dare not hear. Wilt thou find a footstep of the Lord, saith Job, or hast thou attained unto the least things which the Almighty hath made? If the least of his works are incomprehensible, shall he be comprehended who made them all? Eye hath not seen, and ear hath not heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him: if the things which God hath prepared are incomprehensible to our thoughts, how can we comprehend with our mind him who hath prepared them? Then use the next verse for the doctrine of the Spirit. Believe thou also in the Holy Ghost, and hold the same opinion concerning him which thou hast received to hold concerning the Father and the Son, and follow not those who teach blasphemous things of him. Learn thou that this Holy Spirit is One, indivisible, of manifold power, having many operations yet not himself divided; who knoweth the mysteries, who searcheth all things, even the deep things of God; who descended upon the Lord Jesus Christ in form of a dove; who wrought in the Law and in the Prophets; who now also at the season of Baptism sealeth thy soul; of whose holiness every intellectual nature hath need; who with the Father and the Son together is honoured with the glory of the Godhead.

debates: Where the quotation of verse 9 comes from.
Whether the verse describes heaven or the present blessings of the gospel.
Who the us of verse 10 are.
What searching means when said of the Spirit.
outliers: Ellicott argues from the formula it is written that the source must be the Old Testament, and appeals to memory.
Calvin reports two great difficulties in the citation, including that Paul seems to turn the prophet to a foreign purpose.
Robertson dates the revelation to the entry of the gospel into the world rather than to baptism.
Cyril of Jerusalem uses verse 9 to bound what can be known of God and verse 10 to establish the Spirit’s deity.

11.pericope_label: For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God. Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God

schools.summary: Work the analogy and then bound it. The design is to illustrate what has just been said by reference to the way in which a man acquires a knowledge of himself: no man can know his own mind, his own plans and intentions, but himself — his own spirit — and unless he chooses to reveal them to others, they cannot ascertain them. So of God: no man can penetrate his designs, and unless he chooses to make them known by his Spirit they must for ever remain inscrutable to human view. The things of a man are the deep things, the hidden counsels, thoughts, plans, intentions; and by the spirit of man is denoted the human soul, the intellect of man. But it is not to be supposed that there is a perfect resemblance between the relation which the soul of man bears to the man, and the relation which the Holy Spirit bears to God. On the twelfth verse, we means we who are Christians, and especially we the apostles, for the following verse shows he had himself and the other apostles chiefly in view, though it is true of all Christians. Not the spirit of the world means not the wisdom and knowledge which this world can give, not the learning and philosophy so much valued in Greece; and the Spirit is given that we might fully understand and appreciate the favours God has conferred on us in the gospel. It was not only necessary that God should grant the blessings of redemption by the gift of his Son; such was the hardness and blindness of the human heart that it was needful he should grant his Holy Spirit also, that men might be brought fully to see and appreciate the value of those favours, for men do not see them by nature. Elsewhere render it more exactly: who of men knoweth the things of a man? but the spirit of the man which is in him knoweth them. And guard the second clause: these words cannot be taken as an assertion that man cannot have any knowledge of the things of God, but the Apostle urges that man, as man, cannot know the things of God, and that his knowledge of these things is in virtue of his having the Spirit of God dwelling in him. On the twelfth verse, the we must not be confined to the Apostles exclusively: though referring primarily to them, it includes all the members of the Christian Church as one with its teachers and rulers; and the things freely given us of God mean all spiritual things. Elsewhere again keep to the words. Note the two verbs for knowing, the one from the root to see and so to know, the other to know by personal experience, to have come to know and still to know. The spirit of man that is in him is the self-consciousness of man that resides in the man or woman; but note the absence of that phrase with the Spirit of God, for it is not the mere self-consciousness of God, but the personal Holy Spirit in his relation to God the Father. Paul’s analogy between the spirit of man and the Spirit of God does not hold clear through, and he guards it at this vital point, as he does elsewhere. The point here is plain: God’s Holy Spirit is amply qualified to make the revelation claimed in these verses. On the twelfth verse, received is a definite event; the spirit of the world is probably a reference to the wisdom of this age at the sixth verse; and the Spirit which is of God is rather from God, which proceeds from God. That we might know is a purpose clause, and here is a distinct claim of the Holy Spirit for the understanding of the revelation received: it is not a senseless rhapsody or secret mystery, but God expects us to understand the things that are freely given us by God. God gave the revelation through the Holy Spirit, and he gives us the illumination of the Holy Spirit to understand the mind of the Spirit; the tragic failures of men to understand clearly God’s revealed will are but a commentary on the weakness and limitation of the human intellect.

Draw two lessons from the comparison. First, that the doctrine of the Gospel cannot be understood otherwise than by the testimony of the Holy Spirit; and second, that those who have a testimony of this nature from the Holy Spirit have an assurance as firm and solid as if they felt with their hands what they believe, for the Spirit is a faithful and indubitable witness. This is proved by a similitude drawn from ourselves: every one is conscious of his own thoughts, and what lies hid in any man’s heart is unknown to another. In the same way what is the counsel of God, and what his will, is hid from all mankind — who hath been his counsellor? It is therefore a secret recess, inaccessible to mankind; but if the Spirit of God himself introduces us into it, and makes us acquainted with things otherwise hid from our view, there will then be no more ground for hesitation, for nothing that is in God escapes the notice of the Spirit of God. Admit that the similitude may seem not altogether appropriate, since the tongue bears an impress of the mind and mankind communicate their dispositions to each other, so that they become acquainted with each other’s thoughts. On the twelfth verse, heighten by contrast the certainty already mentioned. The Spirit of revelation which we have received is not of the world, so as to be merely creeping upon the ground, so as to be subject to vanity, or be in suspense, or vary or fluctuate, or hold us in doubt and perplexity; on the contrary it is from God, and hence it is above all heavens, of solid and unvarying truth, and placed above all risk of doubt. It is a passage most abundantly clear for refuting that diabolical doctrine as to a constant hesitancy on the part of believers, which requires all believers to be in doubt whether they are in the grace of God or not, and allows of no assurance of salvation but what hangs on moral or probable conjecture. In this they overthrow faith in two respects: they would have us be in doubt whether we are in a state of grace, and then afterwards they suggest an occasion of doubt as to final perseverance. The Apostle declares in general terms that the godly have the Spirit given them, by whose testimony they are assured that they have been adopted to the hope of eternal salvation. Note also what may be meant by the spirit of the world: either Satan, the god of the world, the spirit that is in it and rules over it; or the sinful carnal disposition of the men of the world, which is a spirit of covetousness, uncleanness, pride, malice and error; or rather the carnal wisdom of the world, which is common to worldly men, lies in the knowledge of worldly things, and is pursued for worldly advantages. And note that the thoughts of a man’s heart, the conceptions of his mind, the schemes he is drawing there, his designs, purposes and intentions, can never be known by another man, nor by angels or devils, nor by any creature.

Report the textual question and then apply the verse to the Jews. The word for man in the first clause is omitted by the Alexandrian codex and one other, and by several of the fathers; a bishop contends strongly against its authenticity and reads the passage, for what is there that knoweth the things of a man, except the spirit of a man that is in him? For to say, what man except the spirit of a man, is to speak improperly, and to suppose that the spirit of a man is a man; but it is very proper to say, what except the spirit of a man. Though the authority for omitting the word is comparatively slender, it must be owned that its omission renders the text much more intelligible — and even one manuscript may preserve the true reading. The sense is that a man is conscious of all the schemes, plans and purposes that pass in his own mind, and no man can know these things but himself. Add the inference: all the inmost recesses of his mind, although men are all of one nature and so may the more easily know one another; so the things of God knoweth no one but the Spirit, who, consequently, is God. On the twelfth verse: we who are the genuine apostles of Christ have received this Spirit of God, by which we know the deep things of God, and through the teaching of that Spirit we preach Christ crucified. We have not therefore received the spirit of the world — of the Jewish teachers, who are all looking for a worldly kingdom and a worldly Messiah, and interpret all the scriptures of the Old Testament which relate to him in a carnal and worldly sense. As by princes of the world the apostle means the rulers of the Jews, so by spirit of the world he here means Jewish wisdom, their carnal mode of interpreting the sacred oracles, and their carnal expectation of a worldly kingdom under the Messiah. We receive this teaching that we may know what those supereminently excellent things are which God has purposed freely to give to mankind. And note the distinction: this spirit of the world is not properly received, for the men of the world always had it; but Christians receive the Spirit of God, which before they had not.

Gather the Spirit’s other names. Thou wilt find many titles of the Holy Ghost besides. He is called the Spirit of Holiness, as it is written, according to the Spirit of Holiness. He is also called the Spirit of adoption, as Paul saith, ye received not the spirit of bondage again unto fear, but ye received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. He is also called the Spirit of revelation, as it is written, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him. He is also called the Spirit of promise, as the same Paul says, in whom ye also, after that ye believed, were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise. He is also called the Spirit of grace, as when he says again, and hath done despite to the Spirit of grace. And by many other such titles is he named: in the Psalms he is called at one time the good Spirit, and at another the princely Spirit; and in Isaiah he was styled the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might.

debates: How far the analogy between a man’s spirit and the Spirit of God holds.
Whether the word man belongs in the first clause of verse 11.
What the spirit of the world is.
Whether the we of verse 12 means the apostles only.
outliers: Clarke prefers a reading that drops the word man from the first clause on slender manuscript authority.
Wesley infers from the verse that the Spirit is God.
Calvin turns verse 12 against the doctrine that believers must remain in doubt of their standing in grace.
Wesley denies that the spirit of the world is received at all, since the world always had it.

13.pericope_label: Which things also we speak, not in the words which man’s wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned

schools.summary: Take the verse as a claim to inspiration. Which things also we speak means, which great and glorious and certain truths we, the apostles, preach and explain. Not in the words which man’s wisdom teacheth means not such as human philosophy or eloquence would dictate: they do not have their origin in the devices of human wisdom, nor are they expressed in such words of dazzling and attractive rhetoric as would be employed by those who pride themselves on the wisdom of this world. But which the Holy Ghost teacheth means, in the words which the Holy Ghost imparts to us. Some understand this as referring to the fact that the apostles used the language and expressions which the Holy Ghost had taught in the revelations of the Scriptures, but that is a narrow view: the apostle speaks of the whole course of instruction by which the deep things of God were made known to the Christian church, and all of that was not made known in the very words already contained in the Old Testament. He evidently refers to the fact that the apostles were themselves under the direction of the Holy Spirit in the words and doctrines which they imparted, and this passage is a full proof that they laid claim to divine inspiration. On the natural man, the word stands opposed to spiritual and denotes those who are governed and influenced by the natural instincts, the animal passions and desires, in opposition to those influenced by the Spirit of God. It refers to unregenerate men, but carries also the idea that they are under the influence of the animal passions; the word sensual would correctly express the idea, and it is used by the Greek writers to denote that which man has in common with the brutes, that they are under the influence of the senses or the mere animal nature, in opposition to reason and conscience. Elsewhere insist that the manner as well as the matter is given. Not only the gospel truths themselves, but the very form and manner in which those truths are taught, is the result of spiritual insight. Comparing spiritual things with spiritual is better rendered, explaining spiritual things in spiritual language, which is really only another and more pointed form of what has just been said. The word translated comparing is used in the sense of expounding or teaching in the Septuagint, especially of dreams, where the dream is, so to speak, compared with the interpretation; so here the spiritual things are compared with the spiritual language in which they are stated. Another meaning, explaining spiritual things to spiritual men, has been suggested; but the one adopted seems the more simple and natural, and the other involves a use of the word not found elsewhere in the New Testament. On the natural man, recall that the ordinary manner of speaking of man as consisting of soul and body is altogether inaccurate: true psychology regards man as a trinity of natures, body, soul and spirit — the first our physical nature, the second our intellectual nature, embracing also our desires and human affections, the third our spiritual nature. In each of us there is thus a somatical, a psychical and a pneumatical man, and according as one of those parts dominates the others, so is the character of the individual: one in whom the body is strongest is a carnal or fleshly man, one in whom the intellect or affections predominate is a natural or psychic man, and one in whom the spirit rules — which it can do only when enlightened and guided by the Spirit of God — is a spiritual man. Elsewhere again, name the three stages. There is revelation at the tenth verse, illumination at the twelfth, and inspiration here: Paul claims the help of the Holy Spirit for the reception of the revelation, for the understanding of it, and for the expression of it, and he claimed this authority both for his preaching and for his epistles. The verb rendered speak is onomatopoetic, and in the papyri calls more attention to the form of utterance, while another verb refers more to the substance; but in the New Testament it is used of the highest and holiest speech, and Paul employs it purposely for the utterance of the revelation he has understood.
