Not in words which man’s wisdom teacheth is literally, not in words taught by human wisdom, the verbal adjective being passive and followed by the ablative of source. On the natural man, note the absence of the article, a natural man, an unregenerate man; the adjective is qualitative, from the word for the breath of life, and the Vulgate renders it animal. The same contrast between the natural and the spiritual occurs at the fifteenth chapter: the natural man is the unregenerate man, the spiritual man the renewed man, born again of the Spirit of God. Receiveth not means does not accept, rejects, refuses to accept.

Commend the preaching and then define the man. He is still employed in commending his ministry, and it is a high commendation that he pronounces upon his preaching when he says that it contains a secret revelation of the most important matters — the doctrine of the Holy Spirit, the sum of our salvation, and the inestimable treasures of Christ — that the Corinthians may know how highly it ought to be prized. Meanwhile he returns to the concession he had made before, that his preaching had not been adorned with any glitter of words, and had no lustre of elegance, but was contented with the simple doctrine of the Holy Spirit. By the words of man’s wisdom he means those that savour of human learning, and are polished according to the rules of the rhetoricians, or blown up with philosophical loftiness, with a view to excite the admiration of the hearers; spiritual words, on the other hand, are such as are adapted to a pure and simple style, corresponding to the dignity of the Spirit rather than to an empty ostentation. On the natural man, correct the common opinion. By the natural man he does not mean, as is commonly thought, the man that is given up to gross lusts, or, as they say, to his own sensuality, but any man that is endowed with nothing more than the faculties of nature — a man not endowed with anything more than the natural light of the mind. This appears from the corresponding term, for he draws a comparison between the natural man and the spiritual; and as the spiritual denotes the man whose understanding is regulated by the illumination of the Spirit of God, there can be no doubt that the other denotes the man that is left in a purely natural condition. Note also who is meant: not a babe in Christ, one newly born again, for though such have but little knowledge of spiritual things, yet they have a taste, and do relish and desire and receive the sincere milk of the word, and grow thereby; but an unregenerate man, that has no knowledge at all of such things — and not merely the man openly and notoriously profane, abandoned to sensual lusts and pleasures, though such a one being sensual must be a natural man, but rather the wise philosopher, the Scribe, the disputer of this world, the rationalist, the man of the highest attainments in nature, in whom reason is wrought up to its highest pitch, the man of the greatest natural parts and abilities, yet without the Spirit and grace of God. Indeed, every man in a state of nature, who is as he was born, whatever may be the inward furniture of his mind or his outward conduct of life, is but a natural man.

Say what the apostles could not imitate, and then correct the received rendering. We dare no more use the language of the Jews and the Gentiles in speaking of those glorious things than we can indulge their spirit. The Greek orators affected a high and florid language, full of tropes and figures, which dazzled more than it enlightened; the rabbins affected obscurity, and were studious to find out cabalistical meanings, which had no tendency to make the people wise unto salvation. The apostles could follow none of these: they spoke the things of God in the words of God; everything was plain and intelligible, every word well placed, clear and nervous, and he who has a spiritual mind will easily comprehend an apostle’s preaching. On comparing spiritual things with spiritual: this is commonly understood to mean comparing the spiritual things under the Old Testament with the spiritual things under the New, but this does not appear to be the apostle’s meaning. The word which we translate comparing rather signifies conferring, discussing or explaining, and the other word should be rendered to spiritual men, and not referred to spiritual things; the passage should therefore be translated, explaining spiritual things to spiritual persons — and this sense the following verse absolutely requires. On the natural man: the animal man, the man who is in a mere state of nature and lives under the influence of his animal passions; for the Greek word often translated soul means the lower and sensitive part of man, in opposition to the understanding or rational part, and the Latins use one word to signify these lower passions and another to signify the higher. The person in question is not only one who has had no spiritual teaching, or has not profited by it, but one who lives for the present world, having no respect to spiritual or eternal things; and the animal man is opposed to the spiritual man, who is under the influence of the Spirit of God. Elsewhere put the incapacity in three clauses: receiveth not, that is, does not understand or conceive; neither can he know them, for as he has not the will, so neither has he the power; because they are spiritually discerned, they can only be discerned by the aid of that Spirit, and by those spiritual senses, which he has not. And on the words taught by the Holy Spirit — such are all the words of scripture; how high a regard ought we then to retain for them.

Make the verse a rule for your own teaching. In the preceding Lecture we set before you, our beloved hearers, some small portion of the testimonies concerning the Holy Ghost; and on the present occasion we will, if it be God’s pleasure, proceed to treat of those which remain out of the New Testament; and as then, to keep within due limit of your attention, we restrained our eagerness — for there is no satiety in discoursing concerning the Holy Ghost — so now again we must say but a small part of what remains. For now, as well as then, we candidly own that our weakness is overwhelmed by the multitude of things written. Neither to-day will we use the subtleties of men, for that is unprofitable; but merely call to mind what comes from the divine Scriptures, for this is the safest course, according to the blessed Apostle Paul, who says: Which things also we speak, not in words which man’s wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

debates: Whether comparing spiritual things with spiritual means in spiritual language or to spiritual men.
Whether the apostles claim inspired words as well as inspired matter.
Whether the natural man is the sensual man or simply the unaided man.
Whether man is a duality of soul and body or a trinity of body, soul and spirit.
outliers: Clarke renders the clause, explaining spiritual things to spiritual persons, against the received version.
Ellicott builds a threefold psychology of body, soul and spirit on the word natural.
Calvin denies that the natural man means the man given up to gross lusts.
Robertson names three distinct stages in the passage: revelation, illumination, and inspiration.

15.pericope_label: But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man. For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ

schools.summary: Limit the claim before expounding it. He that is spiritual is the man enlightened by the Holy Spirit, in contradistinction from him who is under the influence of the senses only; judgeth is in the Greek discerneth, the same word as in the previous verse, and means that the spiritual man has a discernment of those truths in regard to which the sensual man was blind and ignorant. All things means not absolutely all things, nor that he is omniscient, but that he has a view of those things to which the apostle had reference, that is, the things revealed to man by the Holy Spirit. Yet he himself is judged is again, is discerned: his feelings, principles, views, hopes, fears and joys cannot be fully understood and appreciated by any natural or sensual man, who does not comprehend the principles that actuate him, does not enter into his joys, does not sympathise with him in his feelings — a matter of simple truth and universal observation. On the sixteenth verse, the passage is quoted from Isaiah, and the interrogative form is a strong mode of denying that any one has ever known the mind of the Lord. The argument is this: no one can understand God, no one can fully comprehend his plans, his feelings, his views, his designs; no one by nature, under the influence of sense and passion, is either disposed to investigate his truths or loves them when they are revealed. But the Christian is influenced by God, has his Spirit, has the mind of Christ, who had the mind of God; he sympathises with Christ, and has his feelings, desires, purposes and plans. And as no one can fully understand God by nature, so neither can he understand him who is influenced by God and is like him; and it is not to be wondered at that he regards the Christian religion as folly, and the Christian as a fool. The mind of Christ means the views, feelings and temper of Christ. Elsewhere put it in a sentence: the spiritual man judges all spiritual truth, but he himself is judged by none who are not spiritual. On the sixteenth verse, take the For as the proof that the enlightened spiritual man cannot be judged by any one who is not thus enlightened: who, thus uninstructed, can know the mind of the Lord Jesus, that he may instruct him? And by we understand spiritual men, including the Apostles. The Apostle here identifies Christ with the Spirit, whom he has previously spoken of as the Teacher of spiritual things; he does not mean to assert that the Apostles knew all that the mind of Christ knew, but that all things which they did know were from him and were spiritual. Elsewhere again press the application. The spiritual man is qualified to sift, to examine, to decide rightly, because he has the eyes of his heart enlightened and is no longer blinded by the god of this world. There is a great lesson here for Christians who know by personal experience the things of the Spirit of God: men of intellectual gifts who are ignorant of the things of Christ talk learnedly and patronisingly about things of which they are grossly ignorant, and the spiritual man is superior to all this false knowledge. Men will pass judgment on him, but the spiritual man refuses to accept the decision of his ignorant judges; he stands superior to them all, as Polycarp did when he preferred to be burnt to saying Lord Caesar in place of Lord Jesus, unwilling to save his earthly life by the worship of Caesar. On the sixteenth verse, the use of the relative is almost consecutive, so that the spiritual man is superior to others who attempt even to instruct God himself; and we have the mind of Christ, as has already been shown, so that all spiritual men are superior to those who try to shake their faith in Christ, the mystery of God.

Say who is not meant before saying who is. Not any particular individual person, and not the pope of Rome, as his adherents vainly imagine, whom they fancy to be a supreme and infallible judge in things spiritual, from whose judgment there is no appeal, and who himself comes not under the judgment of any; for he is so far from being a spiritual man, or having judgment in spiritual things, that he stands described as the man of sin, the son of perdition, the wicked one, the beast, to whom a mouth is given speaking great things and blasphemies. A set of men is here meant, and not such as are only outwardly reformed in their lives and conversations, who are at best but moral and not spiritual men; nor all that have a form of godliness, an appearance of spirituality, for there may be such who have this and yet deny the power of it, in which the principle and essence of spirituality lies; nor all such as have spiritual gifts, which may be where there is no spiritual grace. Then transfer the prerogative from the man to the word. Having stripped of all authority man’s carnal judgment, he teaches that the spiritual alone are fit judges as to this matter, inasmuch as God is known only by his Spirit, and it is his peculiar province to distinguish between his own things and those of others. The meaning is: away with all the discernment of the flesh as to this matter; the Spirit alone has such a firm and solid acquaintance with the mysteries of God as to distinguish without fail between truth and falsehood, between the doctrine of God and the contrivances of man, so as not to fall into mistake. The spiritual man, on the other hand, is judged of none, because the assurance of faith is not subject to men, as though they could make it totter at their nod, it being superior even to angels themselves. Observe that this prerogative is not ascribed to the man as an individual, but to the word of God, which the spiritual follow in judging, and which is truly dictated to them by God with true discernment. On the sixteenth verse, it is probable that Paul had an eye to the fortieth chapter of Isaiah, where the prophet asks who hath been God’s counsellor, who hath aided him in the creation of the world and in his other works, and who hath comprehended the reason of his works. In like manner Paul, by this interrogation, designs to teach that the secret counsel of God which is contained in the gospel is far removed from the understanding of men, and this is a confirmation of the preceding statement. It is uncertain whether he speaks of believers universally or of ministers exclusively; either meaning will suit sufficiently well with the context, though it is preferable to view it as referring more particularly to himself and other faithful ministers. Note also what has not been known: the deep counsels of God’s heart, the scheme of salvation by Jesus Christ as drawn in his eternal mind, the sense of the Spirit of God in the writings of the Old Testament — none of which has any natural man known, by the light of truth or the strength of reason.

Give the plain sense, and then the rival one. He who has the mind of Christ discerns and judges of all things spiritual, yet he himself is not discerned by the mere animal man. Some suppose the verb should be understood thus: he examines, scrutinises, convinces, reproves — a sense it appears to bear elsewhere in this epistle — and they read the verse accordingly: the spiritual man, the well-taught Christian, convinces, that is, can easily convict every animal man of error and vice, yet he himself is convicted of no man, his mind being enlightened and his life holy, so that the animal man cannot convict him of sin. This is a good sense, but the first appears the most natural. Put it also more simply: the spiritual man is he that hath the Spirit, and he discerneth all the things of God whereof we have been speaking, yet is himself discerned by no natural man, for they neither understand what he is nor what he says. On the sixteenth verse, ask the question as the apostle asks it: who that is still an animal man can know the mind of God, so as to instruct the spiritual man? Or better, how can the animal man know the mind of the Lord, and how can any man communicate that knowledge which he has never acquired, and which is foolishness to him because it is spiritual and he is animal? And correct the rendering: the words that he may instruct him should be translated, that he may teach it — that is, the mind of God; not instruct God, but teach his mind to others; and this interpretation the Hebrew will also bear. But we have the mind of Christ: he has endowed us with the same disposition, we being born again by his Spirit, and therefore we are capable of knowing his mind and receiving the teachings of his Spirit; these teachings we do receive, and are therefore well qualified to convey them to others. We are spiritual men, apostles in particular, who know and understand the mind of Christ concerning the whole plan of gospel salvation.

Whether judgeth means discerns or convicts.
Whether that he may instruct him means instruct God or teach God’s mind to others.
Whether we have the mind of Christ is said of all believers or of ministers.
